If these conclusions are correct, they may show us one form of determinism in al-ʿAllāf’s thought.
That would conflict with his well-known Qadarite position: his belief in freedom of choice.
Al-ʿAllāf also introduced another idea into the discussion of the attributes.
He said that God has eternally been hearing and seeing in the sense that he will hear and will see.
The same applies to the other attributes.
All of them are eternal, even though their action may concern things that occur later.
This supports the conclusion we reached above about knowledge.
All the active attributes apply to particular events that come into existence. They are not simply abstract and universal qualities.
But al-ʿAllāf rejects any physical meaning in God’s hearing and sight, following the general Muʿtazilite rejection of anything that would make God bodily.
He gave the attribute of will, however, a separate explanation.
For al-ʿAllāf, God’s will is one thing, while the thing that his will concerns is another.
“His will concerning what he creates is his creation of it, while his creating of a thing is, in his view, different from the thing itself. Creation, for him, is a speech that exists in no place.”
That is, God says to the thing: Be.
But this creative command does not exist in any particular place.
This means that the creative will does not exist within the essence of the creator, nor within the essence of the created thing.
Can we perhaps see here a faint resemblance to Plato’s Forms?

Could this “middle” be something like the separate realities that Plato places between the highest and most perfect Good and the world of appearances and images—that is, the world perceived by the senses?
The resemblance between al-ʿAllāf and Plato on this question is, in our view, too distant to justify concluding that al-ʿAllāf moved toward the Platonic theory of Forms.
Still, it does not rule out the possibility that he was influenced to some extent by Plato’s general picture of a metaphysical world.
We now take another step in the Muʿtazilite discussion of God’s attributes.
A new kind of thinking appears in another Muʿtazilite thinker who lived at the same time as al-ʿAllāf and studied under him: Ibrāhīm ibn Sayyār al-Naẓẓām (d. 221 or 231 AH / 845 CE).
Al-Shahrastānī describes him as someone who:
“read many of the philosophers’ books and mixed their ideas with the teachings of the Muʿtazilites,”
“differed from his fellow Muʿtazilites on a number of questions.”
But al-Naẓẓām’s importance in the Muʿtazilite intellectual tradition goes far beyond the fact that he “read many of the philosophers’ books.”
He built a fairly systematic body of philosophical ideas around many of the major intellectual controversies of his time.
He also seems to have absorbed the culture of his age in remarkable breadth.
“memorized the Qurʾān, the Gospel, the Torah, the Psalms, and their interpretations, in addition to a great amount of poetry, historical reports, and the different legal opinions held by people.”
The early historians of Islamic sects place him among the greatest Muʿtazilite thinkers.
Later and modern Eastern and Western scholars have generally treated him with similar respect.
T. J. de Boer, for example, calls him “a thinker worthy of attention.”
The modern Egyptian Arab scholar Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Hādī Abū Rīda even devoted an entire book to him under the title Ibrāhīm ibn Sayyār al-Naẓẓām and His Theological and Philosophical Views.
For the moment, however, we are interested only in al-Naẓẓām’s position on God’s attributes.
Here he follows the general Muʿtazilite line by rejecting attributes that exist in addition to God’s eternal essence.
But he says that every attribute has two sides.
The positive side affirms the divine essence.
The negative side denies the opposite quality of that essence.
For example, calling God knowing means, on the positive side, affirming God’s essence.
On the negative side, it means denying ignorance of him.
The same principle applies to the other attributes.
Al-Naẓẓām adds another explanation to answer an obvious objection.
If every attribute affirms the divine essence, and the attributes are many, does this not mean that the divine essence itself becomes many?
Would that not contradict divine unity?
Al-Naẓẓām answers that the multiplicity does not come from the positive meaning of the attributes.
It comes from the different negative meanings—the different opposites being denied.
Ignorance, which is the opposite of knowledge, is different from inability, which is the opposite of power, and so on.
But all these opposites are denied of God.
There is therefore no multiplicity in the attributes themselves, and the attributes do not introduce multiplicity into the divine essence.
Al-Naẓẓām did, however, introduce a new position into the Muʿtazilite discussion of one particular attribute: will.

“is not truly described by it”—that is, by will. “When revelation describes him as willing in relation to his own acts, what is meant is that he creates them and brings them into being according to what he knows. When he is described as ‘willing’ the actions of human beings, what is meant is that he commands some of them and forbids others.”
Al-Naẓẓām turns to this special interpretation because he believes that describing God as possessing will in the ordinary and literal sense would imply that God has a need.
Anyone who wants something, in the normal meaning of the word, wants it because he needs what he wants.
God, however, must be free of all need.
Al-Naẓẓām’s view of divine will can therefore be summarized as follows.
When we say that God “willed” something, that thing must be either one of God’s own acts or an act performed by human beings.
If it is one of God’s acts, then God’s “will” toward that act is not really will in the ordinary sense.
It is simply God creating the act directly in accordance with his prior knowledge of it.
There are not two separate things—will and creation.
There is only one: creation, preceded by knowledge of what will be created.
In al-Naẓẓām’s view, then, “will” ultimately comes back to knowledge.
God knows a thing, then creates it.
If, however, the thing that God supposedly “wills” is a human action, it is not accurate to say that God willed the action.
What we should say instead is that God informed people about it in one of two ways: either by commanding it or by forbidding it.
There is only command or prohibition.
Al-Ashʿarī summarizes al-Naẓẓām’s position in the following words:

“To describe God as willing the creation of things means that he creates them. His will to create is the act of creating itself. To describe him as willing the actions of his servants means that he commands them, and the command is different from those actions. We say that he now wills the coming of the Hour, and what this means is that he has decreed that Hour and informed us of it.”
The final result of al-Naẓẓām’s view is therefore the denial of divine will as a separate attribute, whether we are speaking of God’s own acts or of human actions.
This denial of divine will may have led al-Naẓẓām to another theory concerning the creation of the universe.
To avoid the complications created by denying will, he argued that creation happened only once.
There were not many separate acts of creation.
The problem of denying divine will toward God’s acts could therefore be reduced to a single act: the one original act of creation.

“created all existing things at once, exactly as they are now: minerals, plants, animals, and human beings. Adam was not created before his descendants. Rather, God concealed some things within others. Earlier and later apply only to their emergence from what contained them, not to their coming into existence.”
According to al-Naẓẓām, every being in our material world—mineral, plant, animal, or human—already came into existence once and at the same time in a single act of creation.
This applies equally to things that seem to us to have existed in the past, things that seem to exist now, and things that seem to come into existence in the future.
No being was created before another, and no being came into existence after another.
Even Adam did not first come into existence and then have descendants who appeared one generation after another, as things seem to us.
Adam and every generation descended from him, from the beginning of creation to its end, all existed together from the first moment of creation.
What appears to us as a continuous series of new beings coming into existence must therefore have another explanation.
For al-Naẓẓām, these are not new acts of coming into existence.
Rather, all beings were concealed within one another from the beginning.
When we observe what seems to be the “existence” of a new mineral, plant, animal, or human being, it is not really a new existence.
